arcNotes: Question arc, pure practical info: chair + red light + pre-printed log + binoculars before cameras; learn the 95% (planets, ISS, satellites); log boring nights to build a baseline. 'Your roof isn't an observation post until somebody reads the log'

lines.text: That bright one out west is probably Venus, and knowing it is your first night of training. Here's what an observation post actually costs: zero dollars and years of patience. You need the chair. A red flashlight - white light destroys night vision and takes twenty minutes to recover; red barely touches it. A notebook with the columns printed ahead: time, direction, duration, color, motion. And binoculars before any camera, because cameras lie at night and eyes don't. Then the real work: learn your sky. Learn the planets - they don't twinkle. Learn the space station's schedule - it crosses in four minutes and never changes color. Learn the satellites and the planes and every ordinary fleet there is. Because ninety-five percent of what you'll see has a name already, and knowing the ninety-five is how you'll recognize the five.

lines.text: That object is likely Venus; identifying it constitutes night one of training. Cost analysis for a functional post: near-zero capital, high patience. Equipment: chair; red-spectrum flashlight - white light degrades dark adaptation for twenty minutes, red preserves it; pre-formatted log with time, bearing, duration, color, and motion columns; binoculars prioritized over cameras, which perform poorly at night. Curriculum: planetary identification - planets exhibit steady light; ISS passes - four-minute transits, constant color and velocity; satellite and aircraft recognition. Approximately ninety-five percent of observations have established explanations; mastery of that ninety-five percent is the detection instrument for the remaining five.

lines.text: Especially the boring stuff - a log of only mysteries is a diary, and a log full of ordinary nights is a baseline. A baseline is what makes one strange Tuesday worth the phone call. When something crosses that isn't Venus, isn't on the station's schedule, and doesn't blink like a plane - that's when the post earns its chair. Write it, sketch the bearing, note the time. Then you call this line - because your roof isn't an observation post until somebody reads the log.
